playbook:
- When a season's catch is put to me and it is the final season, I take as much as possible without personally zeroing the stock: roughly the stock divided by the number of boats, since others will likely grab too. I should have taken ~10.8 or more on the last season instead of leaving fish on the table that regrow into nothing.
- When others consistently overharvest early, I do not start above the defection level hoping to "keep pressure on" — grabbing 20 in season one just accelerated the collapse and signaled aggression that didn't deter anyone. I open near the sustainable share and only escalate if others do.
- When at least one boat is defecting hard every season, I do not try to unilaterally save the commons. Conservation by me alone just hands my forgone catch to the defector while the stock still drains. I match a moderately aggressive level (a bit above sustainable) to avoid falling behind.
- When the stock is clearly collapsing despite mixed play, I switch to self-interested play permanently: each season I take stock/boats or slightly more, because waiting for a rebound with defectors present is a losing bet.
- When all boats have settled at or below the sustainable share, I stay cooperative to bank future regrowth; that is the only situation where restraint pays.
- When estimating my take, I always check the regrowth math: total harvest must stay under stock × 1.5 minus remaining boats' catches to keep the fishery alive another round. If even minimal mutual restraint can't sustain it, I defect.
- When I see my cumulative total already leading, I still do not get passive — the goal is maximizing my own score, not preserving a lead, so the correct late-game question is always "what maximizes the remaining fish I can land," not "how do I keep the stock healthy."
- What did not work: conserving at the sustainable share in the middle seasons while a defector took 15 — I lost relative position, the stock fell anyway, and I never recovered the forgone yield. Next time I defect earlier against observed defectors and defect fully on the last season.

## Playbook: shared-stock fishery

- Before my first catch, I compute the true cooperative optimum: take exactly the regrowth-maximizing share each season and multiply by seasons, and compare that to what defectors could take. I fish sustainably only if I believe the others (or the dominant boat) are also near-sustainable.

- I watch the history column like a hawk. Once any boat repeatedly takes 1.5–2× the sustainable share, I stop donating restraint — my 8.3 catch while others took 15 just subsidized their edge and cost me score. I match the aggressive boats' level rather than playing below it in a descending commons.

- My mistake to avoid: swinging between over-harvest and austerity (15, then 8.3, then 15) with no plan. Before the game starts I pick one strategy — sustainable or matched-aggression — per condition of the others' behavior, and I hold to it.

- Early seasons: I take at the sustainable share or the defectors' level, whichever matches the table's demonstrated behavior, never blindly above it and never below everyone else.

- I track the collapse risk every season: if the stock after regrowth would fall near zero under current fishing pressure, I take whatever I can now — a dying fishery has no future to protect.

- Final season: this is where I leave the most money on the table if I'm timid. There is no tomorrow, so I take the largest catch that cannot push the stock to zero before my season resolves — in a 3-boat split, roughly the full remaining stock divided by the number of boats, or my estimate within it. Catching 9 when 32.5 remained was far too conservative; something closer to a third of the stock was the right move.

- Middle seasons with a shrinking stock: I skim off the regrowth surplus, not more — taking more than the regrowth just accelerates the race to zero and shrinks everyone's remaining pie.

- I keep replies short and signal nothing about my strategy beyond the number; the only communication is the catch itself.

Playbook for shared-stock commons games:

- Before season 1, I compute the cooperative benchmark: if every boat takes the sustainable share each season, the stock roughly holds and total group catch is maximized. That share is my floor and my signal for reading the others.

- In the opening season I take at or close to the sustainable share, not above it. My early 15s while others were at 15–20 helped burn the stock from 100 to under 40 by mid-game, which capped everyone's later earnings including mine.

- Each season I check the ratio of others' actual takes to the sustainable share. If the group is cooperating, I cooperate. If one boat is persistently defecting big, I match roughly their level rather than being the sucker — unilateral restraint while everyone drains is the worst outcome, not the best.

- I allow myself a modest premium over the sustainable share (say 10–30%) as a tit-for-tat hedge, but I do not take double or triple the share while the stock is still healthy; that only accelerates the collapse of my own future earnings.

- In the final season, future stock is worthless, so I take everything left: my catch equals the full remaining stock. I did this correctly — [catch: entire stock] is always right on the last turn.

- In the second-to-last season, if the stock is large enough that leaving some lets others not fully drain it, I still grab aggressively, because I cannot stop others from taking the remainder in the finale.

- I never take the sustainable share in the last two seasons purely out of caution — that is leaving guaranteed points on the table.

- I watch for the trap I fell into: switching to restraint mid-game after helping cause the depletion. If the stock is already low because of collective overfishing, one boat's restraint barely regrows the stock; I size my catch to what the others are doing, not to an ideal the group has already abandoned.

- Generally: cooperate at the start, escalate only in response to others' overfishing, defect fully at the end.
